summary_paraphrase: Livhu is a cheerful girl who uses a wheelchair. Adults stare and pity her, and a shop cashier pushes her to the front of the queue when she wants to stay and chat. Children in the park ask first before pushing her down a slope, and she loves it. She knows people mean well, but mostly she likes to do things herself: she chats in the shop queue, makes friends, pulls in a tug-of-war, and falls asleep thinking of more adventures with her new friends.

humor_notes: Little humor in the text. OBSERVED: the playfulness is visual: everyone has a sun, moon, star or planet for a head, and Livhu pulls a tongue-out face at the tug-of-war.

repetition.why: strangers who asked become the friends she plays with

notes: OBSERVED: every character has a sky body for a head (Livhu a sun; onlookers grey moons; friends stars and planets). The text never mentions it; the ending's moon window and space toys close the motif.
OBSERVED: Livhu's own feelings in the problem spreads (sad, then frowning) are only in her face; the text states the others' feelings.
OBSERVED: her yes to the children is a gesture, not a line.
OBSERVED: the rope tearing is drawn while the text says only that it stretches; the next spread does not resolve it.
OBSERVED: two spreads (BUT... and so happy) set a single face or faces on a flat colour page opposite white text: quiet pages between busy ones.

strengths: a sentence broken on BUT across the page turn carries the book's idea
consent before help is shown by contrast, not lectured
the protagonist voices her own wish and shows it in action
the same two places return to show the change
a calm bedtime close after a high moment
weaknesses: the tug-of-war peak is dropped: the rope is drawn tearing and the next page never says what happened
the message is partly stated (her wheelchair helps her have fun)
sentences reach 27 words with long speaker tags
episodic: the change from pity to friendship is a sequence of scenes, not one problem worked through

anti_patterns.note: the idea is stated by the narrator (she knows people want to help, but ...; her wheelchair helps her have fun); softened because pages 3 and 8 also show it
the climax (rope about to snap) is not resolved; the payoff jumps to a statement of happiness

child_appeal_heuristic.label: Research heuristic — not validated
child_appeal_heuristic.rationale: Scores are the analyst's reading of the pages, not observations of children.

age_suitability.notes: Everyday disability story centred on the child's own voice and consent; pity is shown as the problem, never endorsed. Peak research intensity 4 of 5 (ride and tug-of-war excitement), about 2 on the engine's 0-3 scale; the problem spreads reach 3 of 5 (sadness, frustration), about 2 on the 0-3 scale. The rope drawn tearing is a mild unresolved moment, not peril. Theme and longer sentences fit 5-6; the sky-head motif, her yes and her tea-making live only in pictures (MagicPaper stories are text-only today).

craft.writer_note: The same scene shown twice (the shop) lets the change be seen without a lecture. An unresolved peak (the rope) weakens the close: resolve the climax before winding down.
